scenarios.title: Points versus percent
scenarios.situation: A vendor announces their tool 'improved uptime from 90% to 95%, a 5% improvement.' Your manager repeats the claim in a planning meeting.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the claim?
choices: It confuses percentage points with percent: 90% to 95% is 5 percentage points but a 5.6% relative improvement, and it hides that downtime halved from 10% to 5%
The math is correct and the claim is fine as stated
Uptime cannot be compared across different measurement periods
The claim is wrong because uptime can never exceed 99%
scenarios.why: Percentage points (absolute difference) and percent change (relative difference) are different units, and mixing them is a classic persuasion trick. The honest headline is that downtime was cut in half (10% to 5%), which is actually more impressive than '5% improvement' suggests. Always recompute the base.
scenarios.hint: What happened to downtime, not uptime?

scenarios.title: The average salary
scenarios.situation: A job posting boasts 'average engineer salary $180,000.' You learn the team is five people: four earn $120,000 and the founder pays himself $420,000.
scenarios.prompt: What statistic should you ask for instead?
choices: The median, which is $120,000 here and describes the typical engineer; the mean is distorted by the single outlier
A bigger sample; five people is too few for any statistic
The mode, which is the most scientific average
The average is fine; $180,000 is what you should expect
scenarios.why: The mean is sensitive to outliers; one extreme value drags it far from anyone's actual experience. The median (the middle value) describes the typical case in skewed distributions like salaries. When someone quotes only the mean for a skewed quantity, ask for the median and the distribution.
scenarios.hint: Which number describes what four out of five people actually earn?

scenarios.title: Retry or fail fast
scenarios.situation: A flaky downstream call succeeds 90% of the time per attempt. Each retry costs 2 seconds; a user-visible failure costs roughly 60 seconds of user time. You can retry up to 3 times.
scenarios.prompt: What does expected value say about retrying?
choices: Retry: the expected cost of retries is small (a few seconds) while the expected savings from avoiding failures is large, since failure probability drops to 0.1% after 3 attempts
Never retry; retries add latency to every request
Retry forever until success; eventual success is guaranteed
Fail fast always; users prefer quick errors to slow successes
scenarios.why: Expected value weighs cost by probability: three retries cost at most ~6 seconds in the rare all-fail case, while cutting user-visible failures from 10% to 0.1% (0.1^3). The retry policy wins by orders of magnitude. 'Retry forever' ignores the tail risk of hanging; bounded retries with backoff capture nearly all the benefit.
scenarios.hint: What is the failure probability after three independent attempts?

scenarios.title: The accurate test
scenarios.situation: A security scanner advertises '99% accuracy' at detecting a rare vulnerability that affects 1 in 10,000 hosts. It flags one of your 10,000 servers.
scenarios.prompt: How likely is the flagged server actually vulnerable?
choices: About 1%: with a 1-in-10,000 base rate, the one true positive is swamped by roughly 100 false positives from the 99% specificity
99%, as advertised
50%, since the test could go either way
100%, because a positive is a positive
scenarios.why: This is the base-rate fallacy: accuracy is meaningless without the base rate. With 1 true vulnerable host and a 1% false-positive rate over 9,999 healthy hosts, you expect ~100 false alarms for every true hit, so any single flag is ~1% likely to be real. Rare conditions need extremely specific tests or a second confirmatory test.
scenarios.hint: Out of 10,000 servers, how many false alarms does 99% specificity produce?

scenarios.title: Nine nines of marketing
scenarios.situation: A vendor promises '99.9% uptime SLA' for a service you will depend on. Your service needs 99.9% availability end-to-end and will chain three such vendor services in series.
scenarios.prompt: What does the math say about your end-to-end availability?
choices: About 99.7%: availabilities multiply in series (0.999^3), giving ~43 extra minutes of downtime per month beyond a single 99.9% component
99.9%: the SLA covers the whole chain
99.97%: redundancy across vendors adds nines
100%: SLAs guarantee uptime, not credit payouts
scenarios.why: Availability of series components multiplies: 0.999^3 = 0.997, and 0.3% of a 30-day month is about 2.2 hours of expected downtime versus 43 minutes for a single 99.9% component. Chained dependencies erode nines fast. Also note an SLA is a credit policy, not a reliability guarantee.
scenarios.hint: If each link works 99.9% of the time, what fraction of the time do all three work at once?

scenarios.title: The survey says
scenarios.situation: A team surveys 'are our deploys painful?' Only 40 of 200 engineers respond; 35 say yes. The team lead reports '87% of engineers find deploys painful' and proposes a rewrite.
scenarios.prompt: What is the statistical flaw?
choices: Non-response bias: engineers with painful deploys are far more likely to answer, so the 87% describes respondents, not the engineering org
The sample is too small; 40 responses can never support a percentage
Surveys are unscientific and should never drive decisions
The math is wrong; 35 of 40 is 80%, not 87%
scenarios.why: Voluntary response surveys oversample the motivated, usually the unhappy: the respondents are a self-selected slice, not a random sample. The 87% is valid only for the 40 who replied (20% of the org). Before a rewrite, you need a representative sample or, better, instrumented data on actual deploy pain.
scenarios.hint: Who had the strongest reason to fill out this survey?

scenarios.title: The Math Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Math is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Math?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Math issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Math is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Math supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Math failure in Acad Math.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
evidence: All Math components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: The Capacity Plan
scenarios.situation: Your service handles 1,000 requests/second at peak. The business expects 10x growth in 18 months. Each server handles 200 rps. Servers cost $500/month. The CFO asks for the 18-month infrastructure budget.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right estimate and its honest uncertainty?
choices: ~$300k/month at peak (10k rps ÷ 200 = 50 servers × $500 = $25k... wait, recompute: 10,000/200 = 50 servers, ×$500 = $25,000/month) — present as $20k–$40k/month range accounting for efficiency gains and headroom, with the factor chain shown
$500/month — one server handles 200 rps and we have 1,000, so we are fine
$5M — 10x growth means 10x everything plus safety margin, round up aggressively
Cannot estimate without a detailed architecture review — refuse to answer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The math: 10,000 rps ÷ 200 rps/server = 50 servers × $500 = $25,000/month. But honest estimation adds: efficiency may improve (fewer servers), headroom is needed (more servers), growth may be uneven. Present $20k–$40k with the chain visible. The CFO needs the exponent ($10^4/month) and the drivers, not false precision. Note the self-correction in the chain — showing your work catches arithmetic slips.
scenarios.hint: Did you show the factor chain or just the answer?

scenarios.title: The A/B Test Reading
scenarios.situation: An A/B test shows variant B converts 5.2% vs A's 5.0% — a 4% relative lift. The test ran 3 days with 2,000 visitors per variant. Product wants to ship B immediately.
scenarios.prompt: Should you ship?
choices: No — 2,000 visitors per variant is underpowered for a 0.2pp absolute difference; the result is likely noise. Calculate: detecting a 4% relative lift at 5% base needs ~100k+ visitors per variant for 80% power. Keep running
Yes — 5.2% beats 5.0%, the data is clear
Ship B but also keep A — run both permanently to be safe
The test is rigged — 4% lifts do not happen in 3 days
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A 0.2 percentage-point difference with n=2,000 per arm has a standard error around 0.7pp — the 'lift' is well within noise. This is the most common statistical error in product: shipping noise as signal. The fix is pre-registered sample sizes from power analysis, not peeking at 3 days. Underpowered tests produce false positives that compound into bad roadmaps.
scenarios.hint: Is the difference bigger than the noise?
objectives: Require power analysis before A/B tests
Distinguish signal from noise in small samples

scenarios.title: The Base Rate Neglect
scenarios.situation: A security tool flags 1% of logins as 'suspicious' with 99% accuracy. Your site has 1M logins/day. The SOC wants to investigate every flag. You do the math.
scenarios.prompt: How many daily flags are false alarms?
choices: ~10,000 flags/day, and the vast majority are false positives: even at 99% accuracy, with a 1% flag rate on 1M logins you get ~10k flags; if true attacks are 1 in 10,000 logins (100/day), then ~9,900 of 10,000 flags are false — the base rate dominates
100 — 99% accuracy means only 1% are wrong
10,000 and all are real — the tool is 99% accurate
Zero — 99% accuracy means no false alarms
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Base rate neglect is the classic error: 99% accuracy sounds excellent until you multiply by 1M events. With 100 true attacks among 1M logins, the tool flags ~10,000 (1%), of which ~99 are true positives and ~9,901 are false. The SOC investigating all 10k burns out in a week. The fix: tune thresholds by base rate, layer signals, and never deploy detection without base-rate math.
scenarios.hint: Does 99% accuracy survive contact with 1M events?
objectives: Apply base rates to detection math
Tune alerting by expected false positives

scenarios.title: The Expected Value Bet
scenarios.situation: A vendor offers a $50k 'performance guarantee' insurance: if your launch misses its SLA, they pay $500k. Your internal estimate says 10% chance of missing SLA. Finance asks if you should buy it.
scenarios.prompt: What does expected value say?
choices: EV = 0.10 × $500k − $50k = $0 — actuarially fair, so decide on risk tolerance: buy it if a $500k miss would be existential (insurance value), skip it if you can absorb the miss (keep the premium)
Buy it — $500k payout dwarfs the $50k cost
Skip it — 90% chance you waste $50k
Negotiate the premium down — $50k is too much regardless
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. EV = $50k − $50k = $0: the price is fair. Fair-priced insurance is bought for risk transfer, not profit — if a $500k miss kills the company, $50k is cheap survival; if the miss is absorbable, keep the premium. Most technology decisions hide this math: compute EV, then decide by risk tolerance, not by fear or greed.
scenarios.hint: Is this a profit decision or a survival decision?
objectives: Separate actuarial fairness from risk tolerance

scenarios.title: The P99 Deception
scenarios.situation: Your API dashboard shows p50 latency 40ms, p99 800ms. The team celebrates: '99% of requests are fast!' Support tickets about slowness keep rising. Traffic is 10M requests/day.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the celebration wrong?
choices: 1% of 10M is 100,000 slow requests daily — p99 hides 100k bad experiences. Report the count, not just the percentile: '100k requests/day exceed 800ms' reframes the problem from '1%' to 'a city's worth of users'
p99 is the wrong metric — only p50 matters
The dashboard is lying — percentiles cannot be trusted
800ms is fine — users cannot perceive sub-second latency
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Percentiles hide counts: 1% sounds tiny until multiplied by scale. 100,000 slow requests/day is a support-ticket factory. The discipline: always convert tail percentiles to absolute counts at your traffic. 'p99 800ms' is abstract; '100k users/day wait 800ms+' is actionable. Tail latency is where user trust dies, one slow request at a time.
scenarios.hint: What is 1% multiplied by your traffic?
objectives: Convert tail percentiles to absolute counts
Measure user impact, not just percentages

scenarios.title: The Survey Trap
scenarios.situation: A survey of your 50 most active users shows 90% want feature X. The product team wants to prioritize X for all 10,000 users. You notice the survey went to power users only.
scenarios.prompt: What is the statistical problem?
choices: Selection bias: power users are not representative — they have different needs, tolerance, and workflows than the silent majority. 90% of a biased sample tells you about the sample, not the population. Survey the quiet 9,950 before prioritizing
90% is overwhelming — ship feature X immediately
Survey 50 more power users to confirm — bigger sample fixes it
Ignore surveys entirely — users do not know what they want
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Bigger biased samples produce more confident wrong answers — 100 power users still are not the 9,950 silent ones. The fix is stratified sampling: survey across activity tiers, or better, instrument actual behavior (what do the quiet users click?). Stated preference from enthusiasts ≠ revealed preference of the majority. Every survey result needs the question: 'who did we NOT hear from?'
scenarios.hint: Who is missing from the sample?

lessons.title: Math — Core concepts
concepts: Estimate before you calculate: orders of magnitude and back-of-envelope arithmetic catch absurdities that precise spreadsheets hide.
Expected value decides under uncertainty: multiply each outcome by its probability and sum; feelings about risk are no substitute for the arithmetic.
Respect the base rate: a test's accuracy means nothing without the prevalence of what it detects; rare conditions make most positives false positives.
Distrust lonely averages: in skewed data the median describes the typical case; always ask what the distribution looks like.
Percentages need bases: percentage points, percent change, and the original denominator are three different things, and persuasion lives in the confusion.
Samples must represent: voluntary, convenient, and survivorship-biased samples describe themselves, not the population; ask who is missing.

example.walkthrough: Expected value in one line: a 90% chance of gaining 200 against a 10% chance of losing 1000 is worth 80. Write the equation before deciding; the gut cannot do this arithmetic reliably.

pitfalls: Common trap: averaging averages from different-sized groups, which weights small groups equally with large ones.
Common trap: reading P(positive test | disease) as P(disease | positive test); the base rate flips the meaning.
Common trap: survivorship bias; studying only the winners (successful startups, surviving servers) hides the base rate of failure.
Common trap: adding percentages that have different bases, which produces nonsense totals.

lessons.title: Fermi Estimation
concepts: Break impossible questions into multiplied guesses: each guess within 10x, and errors cancel across 4-5 factors to land within 2-3x of truth.
Round aggressively: use powers of 10 and simple numbers. Precision in inputs you guessed is theater — 3 × 10^6 beats 3,141,592 when the 3 was a guess.
Calibrate with known anchors: US population ~3×10^8, seconds/year ~3×10^7 (π×10^7), engineers at big tech ~10^5. Anchor, then scale.
The goal is the exponent, not the mantissa: knowing it is ~10^6 vs ~10^9 decides architectures. The exact digits rarely matter.

example.code:
FERMI: piano tuners in Chicago
Population: 3×10^6
Households (÷2.5): ~10^6
Pianos per household: 1 in 20 → 5×10^4
Tuned yearly: 1 in 3 → ~2×10^4
Tunings per tuner/year: 1000
Tuners: ~20

Actual: ~30. Exponent right.
Method beats precision.
example.walkthrough: Estimate something today: how many engineers at your company? How much storage does your team use? Show the factor chain.

pitfalls: False precision: 5 significant figures on guessed inputs
Skipping the factor chain — jumping to the answer without decomposition
Never checking against reality — Fermi without calibration drifts

lessons.title: Order-of-Magnitude Sanity Checks
concepts: Before trusting any number, ask: is the exponent plausible? A $10M cloud bill for a 10-person startup fails the smell test at 10^7.
Unit analysis catches errors: if your 'requests per second' computes to requests×seconds, the formula is wrong regardless of the digits.
Compare against anchors: storage in exabytes for a blog, latency in nanoseconds across continents — impossible exponents reveal broken assumptions.
Build the habit: every dashboard number gets 5 seconds of 'does 10^x make sense here?' before any deeper analysis.

example.code:
SANITY FAILS
'This query scans 10^15 rows'
  → 1 petarow; your table has 10^8.
  Something is very wrong.

'API latency p99: 3 nanoseconds'
  → light travels 1m in 3ns.
  Your datacenter is bigger than 1m.

'Training cost: $12'
  → GPU-hours alone exceed this.
  Missing 3+ orders of magnitude.
example.walkthrough: Take three numbers from your work this week. Sanity-check each exponent in 30 seconds. Flag any that fail.

pitfalls: Accepting dashboard numbers as ground truth — dashboards compute, they do not think
Unit blindness: comparing ms to seconds without converting
Anchoring on the first number seen instead of independent estimation

lessons.title: Breaking Down Big Numbers
concepts: Decompose multiplicatively: total = count × average. Users × queries/user, servers × cost/server, rows × bytes/row. Two easy guesses beat one hard one.
Decompose additively for budgets: total = sum of parts. List every component, estimate each, sum. Missing components are found by asking 'what else?'
Use ranges, not points: '10-50ms' is more honest than '27ms' when uncertain. Propagate ranges through the math to get honest bounds.
Identify the dominant term: in most estimates, one factor drives 80% of the result. Get that one right; the rest can be rough.

example.code:
DECOMPOSITION
Monthly infra cost:
  Compute: 200 VMs × $50 = $10k
  Storage: 50TB × $20/TB = $1k
  Transfer: 10TB × $90/TB = $900
  Managed DB: 3 × $400 = $1.2k
  Total ≈ $13k/month

Dominant: compute (77%).
Optimize there first.

Range version: $10k–$18k
(honest about VM count uncertainty)

pitfalls: Single-point estimates presented as facts — hiding uncertainty
Missing components: the 'what else?' question asked zero times
Optimizing the 5% term while ignoring the 80% term

lessons.title: Estimation in Interviews

Round to friendly numbers immediately: 7.8 billion → 10^10, 330 million → 3×10^8. The interviewer wants the method, and round numbers keep you fluent.
Sanity-check at the end: 'does ~10^4 make sense?' A 10-second gut check catches factor errors and shows judgment.

Factor 3: [frequency] ≈ [10^z]

lessons.title: Probability Rules That Matter
concepts: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B): subtract the overlap or you double-count — most probability errors are double-counting.
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A): chain rule. For independent events it simplifies to P(A) × P(B), but independence is a claim you must justify, not assume.
Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Often the easiest path — computing the chance nothing fails is simpler than enumerating every failure.
Sanity bound: every probability lives in [0, 1]. If your computed answer is negative or above 1, the arithmetic is wrong — check before interpreting.

example.code:
# Probability Rules That Matter
#

lessons.title: Poisson: Counting Random Events
concepts: Poisson models event counts in fixed intervals: requests per second, errors per hour, arrivals per minute. One parameter: λ (the average rate).
Key property: variance = mean = λ. If your observed variance >> mean, events are bursty (not Poisson) — look for the clustering cause.

Poisson assumes independence: one request doesn't cause another. Retry storms and cascading failures violate this — model those separately.

lessons.title: Exponential: Waiting Times
concepts: Exponential models time between Poisson events: time to next failure, time between arrivals. Memoryless — the expected wait doesn't shrink because you've waited.
Memoryless means no 'due for a failure': a 5-year-old disk with exponential failure is no more likely to fail tomorrow than a new one. (Real disks wear out — that's Weibull, not exponential.)
MTTF/MTBF math: with exponential failures, P(survive t) = e^(-t/MTTF). A 100k-hour MTTF drive has ~8.4% annual failure probability.
Queueing theory builds on exponential: M/M/1 queues assume exponential arrivals and service. Know when the assumption holds (it often roughly does for human-driven arrivals).

simulations.title: The 99% accurate test
simulations.brief: A vendor pitches a threat-detection tool: '99% accurate!' Your CISO wants to buy it for the SOC. You run the numbers. Decide.

steps.symptom: The tool is 99% accurate: 99% true-positive rate, 1% false-positive rate. Real attacks are rare: 1 in 10,000 events is an actual attack.
evidence:
True positive rate: 99% | false positive rate: 1%
Base rate: 1 real attack per 10,000 events
CISO: '99% accurate — let's buy it'
options: Buy it — 99% accuracy speaks for itself
Run the base-rate math first: with 10,000 events, expect ~1 true alarm and ~100 false alarms — so a positive alert is ~1% likely to be real
Ask for a demo instead of doing math
Reject it — no tool is 99% accurate
steps.explain: The base rate dominates: 1 true positive drowns in ~100 false positives, so P(attack | alert) is about 1%, not 99%. 'Accuracy' without the base rate is a marketing number. Always multiply by the base rate before you buy — or believe.

steps.symptom: The math is done: 99% 'accurate', ~1% useful. The vendor counters: 'But it catches 99% of real attacks!'
evidence:
Vendor: 'Missing attacks is worse than false alarms.'
SOC capacity: 3 analysts, ~40 alerts/day sustainable
options: Buy it — catching attacks matters most
Decline on capacity math: ~100 false alarms/day buries 3 analysts, so real attacks get missed in the noise — the tool makes detection worse, not better
Buy it but turn off the alerts
Hire 20 more analysts to handle the alerts
steps.explain: A detector your team cannot keep up with is not a detector — it is a noise machine that hides the real signal. Expected value includes the cost of acting on the output: 100 false alarms a day at 3 analysts means the 1 true positive dies unread.

steps.symptom: Declined. The CISO asks what a good detection investment looks like.
options: 'Nothing — detection is hopeless.'
'Invest where the base rate is favorable: high-signal detections on crown-jewel assets, tuned to our environment, measured by precision in production — not vendor accuracy claims.'
'The cheapest tool.'
'Whatever our competitors bought.'
steps.explain: Good security spending follows the math: concentrate detection where attacks are likeliest and signals are cleanest, and evaluate on precision in YOUR environment. The lesson generalizes: never buy a rate without asking 'rate of what, out of what?'

simulations.debrief: You multiplied by the base rate, priced the false alarms in analyst-hours, and redirected the budget to high-signal detection. Base-rate neglect is the most expensive innumeracy in technology.

simulations.title: Expected value of the outage
simulations.brief: A redundancy project costs $80k. Without it, a regional outage costs $500k and happens 'every few years.' Finance wants a yes or no with numbers. Decide with expected value.

steps.symptom: Project cost: $80k one-time. Outage cost: $500k per event. Historical frequency: roughly once every 4 years.
evidence:
Redundancy: $80k once
Outage: $500k/event, ~1 per 4 years
Finance: 'Show me the math'
options: '$500k is bigger than $80k, so yes.'
Compute expected annual loss: $500k / 4 = $125k/year. The $80k project pays for itself in under a year of expected loss — yes, with margin
'Outages are rare, so no.'
Ask for a consultant's opinion
steps.explain: Expected value turns vibes into arithmetic: $125k/year of expected loss versus a one-time $80k. The project pays back in about 8 months of risk. 'Every few years' felt rare; $125k/year does not.

steps.symptom: Finance pushes back: 'Your 1-in-4-years is a guess. What if it is 1 in 10?'
evidence: Finance: 'If the real rate is 1 in 10 years, the math flips.'
options: Insist the 1-in-4 estimate is right

Do the sensitivity analysis: at 1 in 10 years the expected loss is $50k/year — still positive over a 2-year horizon, and the break-even rate is 1 in 6.25 years. Show the range, not just the point estimate
Abandon the project — they might be right
Find data that supports 1-in-4
steps.explain: Point estimates are fragile; ranges are honest. The sensitivity analysis shows the decision survives even pessimistic assumptions (break-even at 1 in 6.25 years). Decisions under uncertainty get ranges, not false precision.

steps.symptom: Approved. But finance adds: 'If no outage happens in 2 years, was the $80k wasted?'
evidence: Finance: 'How will we know it was worth it?'
options: 'We won't — that's the deal.'
'We judge the decision by the information at the time, not the outcome. Fire insurance isn't wasted if the house doesn't burn — and we'll also track leading indicators like failover drill times.'
'If nothing happens, I'll admit it was wasted.'
Promise an outage to prove the value
steps.explain: Good decisions can have quiet outcomes — that is what insurance means. You evaluate the bet by its expected value at decision time, and you track leading indicators (drill performance) so the capability stays real even when the event stays hypothetical.

simulations.debrief: You priced the risk, stress-tested the estimate, and defended the decision against outcome bias. Expected value is how adults buy down risk.

simulations.title: The misleading average
simulations.brief: The dashboard says average latency is 120ms — excellent. Users say the app feels broken. Both are telling the truth. Find the statistic that lies.

steps.symptom: Mean latency: 120ms. User complaints: 'every few minutes it hangs for seconds.' The dashboard is green.
evidence:
Mean latency: 120ms (SLO: <200ms) — green
Complaints: periodic multi-second hangs
Sample: 10,000 requests
options: Trust the dashboard — the users are exaggerating
Look at the distribution, not the mean: check p95/p99 and the histogram — a good mean can hide a terrible tail
Lower the SLO to make the dashboard honest
Add more servers
steps.explain: The mean is a liar when distributions skew: 9,900 fast requests and 100 horrible ones average to 'fine.' Users live in the tail, not the mean. Percentiles (p95, p99) describe experience; means describe arithmetic.

steps.symptom: p99 is 4.2 seconds. The histogram shows a clean fast cluster and a long ugly tail — periodic, every few minutes.
evidence:
p50: 80ms | p95: 300ms | p99: 4.2s
Pattern: tail spikes every ~5 minutes, then recovers
options: Report the p99 and call it a day
Hypothesize from the periodicity: a 5-minute cycle smells like GC pauses, cron jobs, or cache expiry — correlate the spikes with system events
Average the p99 away with more samples
Tell users the p99 is acceptable
steps.explain: Periodicity is a fingerprint: 5-minute cycles point at scheduled causes (GC, cron, expiry), not random ones. The statistic told you where to look; the pattern tells you what to suspect. Diagnose the tail, not the average.

steps.symptom: Found: a cron job every 5 minutes locks a table the requests need. Fixed. What changes about the dashboard?
evidence:
Cron rescheduled off-peak, lock removed
p99: 4.2s -> 210ms
options: Keep the mean dashboard — it is green again
Replace the mean with p50/p95/p99 on the dashboard, and alert on the tail — the mean hid this for weeks
Delete the latency dashboard
Set the SLO on the mean, tighter
steps.explain: The dashboard was not wrong, it was the wrong statistic. Percentiles on the dashboard, alerts on the tail: measure what users feel. The mean can stay as a footnote.

simulations.debrief: You distrusted the mean, read the distribution, used periodicity as a fingerprint, and fixed the dashboard's statistic. Averages summarize; percentiles testify.

simulations.title: A/B test or noise?
simulations.brief: The new checkout flow converted 5.2% vs 4.9% for the old — over 3 days, 2,000 users per side. Product wants to ship it. Is it real?

steps.symptom: Variant B: 5.2% (104/2000). Control A: 4.9% (98/2000). Three days of data. Product: 'Ship it, B wins.'
evidence:
A: 98/2000 = 4.9% | B: 104/2000 = 5.2%
Duration: 3 days | Product: 'B wins, ship it'
options: Ship B — 5.2 is bigger than 4.9
Check significance first: a 6-conversion gap on 2,000 users is well within noise — run the test longer or accept you cannot tell
Ship B but watch it
Declare the test inconclusive and never test again
steps.explain: Six conversions out of two thousand is noise wearing a costume. With this sample size, the standard error swallows the 0.3-point gap — you cannot distinguish B's 'win' from a coin flip. Shipping on noise means shipping randomly.

steps.symptom: You explain it is noise. Product asks: 'How long until we know?'
evidence: Product: 'How many users do we need?'
options: 'A few more days should do it.'
Do the power math: detecting a 0.3-point lift at 5% base needs roughly 100k+ users per side — weeks, not days. Offer the real trade: run longer, accept a bigger minimum effect, or test bigger changes
'Statistics can't answer that.'
Peek at the data daily and ship when it looks good
steps.explain: Small effects need big samples — that is the iron law. Give the real number (order of 100k per side for a 0.3-point lift) and the real options: longer run, bigger minimum detectable effect, or bolder variants. And never peek-and-ship: peeking inflates false positives.

steps.symptom: The test runs to full power: B wins by 0.4 points, significant. Product wants to ship and move on.
evidence:
B: +0.4pts, p < 0.05, full power
Product: 'Ship it'
options: Ship and forget
Ship, but record the effect size honestly: a real but small win — and bank the learning about what moves checkout
Keep testing B variants forever
Question the p-value
steps.explain: Significant is not the same as important: +0.4 points is real and worth shipping, but it is a small win, not a breakthrough. Record the effect size, bank the learning, and keep hunting bigger levers. Statistics tells you it is real; judgment tells you what it is worth.

simulations.debrief: You refused to ship on noise, priced the sample size honestly, and treated significance as the start of judgment, not the end. Most 'wins' are noise — the math tells you which.

simulations.title: Fermi the migration
simulations.brief: The CTO asks in the hallway: 'Roughly what will the cloud migration cost per month?' You have 30 seconds and no spreadsheet. Estimate like a physicist.

steps.symptom: Hallway, CTO, 30 seconds: 'Ballpark the monthly cloud cost for the migration.' You know: ~60 VMs, mostly idle.
evidence:
~60 VMs | mostly idle web/app servers
CTO wants: order of magnitude, now
options: 'I'll get back to you with a spreadsheet.'
Fermi it: 60 VMs x ~$50/month average (mix of small sizes, mostly idle) = ~$3k/month compute, double for storage/transfer overhead -> ~$5-10k/month ballpark
'Probably around a million.'
'It depends.'
steps.explain: Fermi estimation is decomposition with round numbers: count the units, price a typical unit, multiply, add an overhead factor, state the range. $5-10k/month is a decision-useful ballpark in 30 seconds; 'I'll get back to you' is a decision delayed.

steps.symptom: CTO: 'Is that high or low? I need to know if we're in trouble.'
options: 'It's just an estimate.'
Anchor it: 'Current data-center run-rate is ~$25k/month, so $5-10k is a reduction — but the estimate's uncertainty is 2x, and data transfer is the wild card. I'll firm it up this week.'
'We're definitely fine.'
Refuse to compare without more data
steps.explain: Estimates need anchors and uncertainty bars: compare to the known $25k, state the 2x uncertainty honestly, name the biggest unknown (transfer). A ballpark with error bars beats a precise number built on guesses.

steps.symptom: Back at your desk: how do you firm up the Fermi estimate properly?
evidence: Turn the hallway math into a real estimate
options: Keep the hallway number — it was fine
Replace each Fermi factor with measured data: actual VM sizes from the inventory, real utilization from monitoring, priced with the provider calculator, plus a 20% contingency
Ask the vendor for a quote and trust it
Add 50% to be safe and present that
steps.explain: Fermi estimates get refined factor by factor: inventory replaces the VM guess, monitoring replaces the utilization guess, the price calculator replaces the $50 guess. Keep the structure, upgrade the inputs — and keep the contingency explicit, not hidden.

simulations.debrief: You estimated under pressure with round numbers, anchored with uncertainty, and knew exactly how to refine it. Fermi estimation is not guessing — it is structured, upgradable guessing.

consoleSims.title: Measure the experiment
consoleSims.brief: The A/B test needs a measurements table. Create it with an id, a value, and a taken_at — then write a query computing the average value. The console checks your SQL actually averages.

tasks.instruction: Create a table named measurements with columns: id INTEGER, value REAL, taken_at TEXT.

params.name: measurements
params.columns: id INTEGER, value REAL, taken_at TEXT

tasks.hint: Create table: NAME=measurements, COLUMNS='id INTEGER, value REAL, taken_at TEXT'.

tasks.instruction: Run a SQL query that averages the value column (use AVG).
tasks.hint: Type a query containing AVG, e.g. SELECT AVG(value) FROM measurements.

consoleSims.debrief: Schema for the experiment, then the average — but remember the misleading-average simulation: AVG is the start of the analysis, never the end.

consoleSims.title: Breakpoint the accumulator
consoleSims.brief: You are debugging a statistics script. Open app.py and set a breakpoint on line 4 — where the accumulator grows — so you can watch the sum evolve.

tasks.instruction: Set a breakpoint on line 4 of app.py.
tasks.hint: Toggle a breakpoint: FILE=app.py, LINE=4 (the accumulator line).

consoleSims.debrief: Breakpoints are how you watch math happen. Set them where the state changes — accumulators, loop variables, running totals.

consoleSims.title: File the estimation worksheet
consoleSims.brief: Fermi estimates deserve to be written down. Title the worksheet, set the owner contact, and submit it — estimates with owners get refined; others evaporate.

tasks.instruction: Set the site_name field to 'Estimation worksheet'.

consoleSims.debrief: Written estimates beat remembered ones. The worksheet is where the hallway math becomes a plan.

consoleSims.title: Filter the measurements
consoleSims.brief: Averages lie when the sample is polluted. Index the taken_at column of measurements for time-window queries, then write a query that filters with WHERE.

tasks.instruction: Create an index on the taken_at column of measurements.
Run a SQL query that filters measurements with a WHERE clause.
tasks.hint: Type a query containing WHERE, e.g. SELECT * FROM measurements WHERE value > 100.

consoleSims.debrief: Filter before you average. The WHERE clause is where data quality lives — every honest analysis starts by defining the sample.

terminalMissions.title: Who is calculating
terminalMissions.brief: Calculations have authors. Print your username.

checks.hint: Run: whoami — who is calculating?

terminalMissions.title: List the data files
terminalMissions.brief: Quantitative work starts with the data at hand. List the home directory.

checks.hint: Run: ls — list the data files.

terminalMissions.success_message: Data listed. Measure what is here before estimating what is not.

terminalMissions.title: State the estimate
terminalMissions.brief: Fermi estimate: 60 VMs at ~$50/month = $3,000/month compute. State the number with echo — estimates get stated, not mumbled.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the estimate (e.g. echo "estimate 3000 per month").

terminalMissions.success_message: Estimate stated. A stated number can be checked; a mumbled one cannot.

terminalMissions.title: State the base rate
terminalMissions.brief: Two errors in six log lines: the base rate is ~33%. State it with echo — base rates get written down.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the base rate (e.g. echo "base rate 33 percent").

terminalMissions.success_message: Base rate stated. The first thing people forget and the last thing that matters.

terminalMissions.title: Name the host
terminalMissions.brief: Even math runs somewhere. Print the hostname.

checks.hint: Run: hostname — name the host.

terminalMissions.success_message: Host named. Context is part of the calculation.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the platform
terminalMissions.brief: Print the full system information — the instrument gets calibrated.

checks.hint: Run: uname -a — calibrate the instrument.

terminalMissions.success_message: Instrument calibrated. Know what you compute on.

terminalMissions.title: Sign the proof
terminalMissions.brief: Conclude with QED via echo, then print your identity record — the prover signs the proof.

checks.hint: Run: echo QED — conclude the proof.
Run: id — sign the proof.

terminalMissions.success_message: QED, signed. A proof without a prover is just a rumor with notation.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.

Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before

Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.

Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one

Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.

How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood

Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.

The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed

No measurable outcome

No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
